title: the tenth guru, the khalsa, the saint-soldier
hookLine: the tenth Guru, the Khalsa, the saint-soldier
tomorrow: a scripture that is the guru
last: THE FIVE KS — REMINDERS YOU CAN TOUCH.

lines: A FATHER WHO DOESN'T COME BACK.
cards: Nine years old. A father leaving home, knowing he may not come back. He has gone to the capital to stand up for the right of people from another faith to practice theirs, and he doesn't come back.

Now the community turns to the boy and tells him: you are the Guru. That's how the tenth Guru's leadership began, in 1675, as Sikh tradition tells it. The boy grew into a poet, a warrior and the founder of the Khalsa.

teach.h: THE TENTH AND LAST HUMAN GURU.
teach.b: Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth and last human Guru of the Sikhs.

teach.h: A FATHER WHO DIED FOR OTHERS' FREEDOM.
teach.b: His father was the ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur. Sikh tradition remembers that he went to Delhi on behalf of Hindu Kashmiri pandits who were being pressed to convert, and was executed there by the Mughal authorities.
Sikhs honor him as a martyr who gave his life for the freedom of others to worship. That memory shaped his son. Guru Gobind Singh taught that a person of faith should be two things at once.
The Sikh phrase is sant sipahi: saint and soldier.

Saint, because the inner life comes first: remembrance, humility, the name. Soldier, because when the weak are being crushed, a saint doesn't look away. The kirpan from yesterday comes from exactly this.
And the order matters. A soldier with no saint in him is only violence; a saint with no courage may stand by while others suffer.
He wrote devotional poetry Sikhs still recite every day, and in 1699 he called the five from day four out of the crowd.
He lost his father, and all four of his sons, to the violence of his time, and is still remembered for chardi kala. And near the end of his life he decided there would be no eleventh human Guru.

how: Sikhs honor Guru Gobind Singh as the tenth Guru and founder of the Khalsa, celebrate his birth each year, recite his compositions in daily prayers, and speak of the ideal of the sant sipahi, the saint-soldier.

p: where the great gathering was held

s: Guru Gobind Singh was only a warrior
he was a poet too; Sikhs recite his writing every day.
his father was executed for defending others' freedom to worship
tradition remembers Guru Tegh Bahadur standing up for Kashmiri pandits.
in the saint-soldier, the soldier comes first
the saint comes first. courage serves the inner life, not the other way round.

games.q: you're a person of deep prayer, and you see the weak being crushed. what does the saint-soldier do?
o: pray, and stay out of it.
stand up for them, with the saint first.
games.why: sant sipahi: saint first, then soldier. a saint doesn't look away, and a soldier without the saint is only violence.

practice: Let one hand rest open on your lap: that's the saint, quiet, open, remembering. Let the other close into a gentle fist: that's the courage to stand up for someone. Feel both at once.
Now think of one person in your life who might need someone to stand up for them, and hold them in mind, with both hands.

wordCard.voice: Guru Gobind Singh. The tenth Guru, founder of the Khalsa, poet and warrior: the saint-soldier. Nineteenth word.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: the tenth Guru. Singh means lion, the name taken by Khalsa men.

carryVoice: Your line: sword and saint. The saint comes first, and the courage serves it. Day nineteen.
